quickAnswer: Indian philosophy offers many carefully argued answers. Advaita holds that only Brahman is ultimately real and the world is an appearance (maya); Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita treat the world as fully real, either as God's body or as eternally distinct from God. Sankhya counts two realities, consciousness and nature; Nyaya-Vaisheshika lists categories of real things; Buddhist schools speak of impermanence, dependent origination and emptiness; Jainism insists reality is many-sided. Each answer is tied to a theory of how we know.

perspectives.view: Advaita holds that Brahman, pure being-consciousness, alone is ultimately real; the world of many things is neither simply real nor simply unreal but an appearance (maya) superimposed on Brahman.
Ramanuja holds that the world and selves are real and form the body of Brahman; reality is one, but internally differentiated.
Sankhya describes two fundamental realities: many conscious purushas and a single unconscious prakriti whose evolutes make up mind and matter.
Vaisheshika analyses reality into categories (padarthas) such as substance, quality and action, with atoms as the ultimate constituents of material things.
Nagarjuna argues that all things are empty (shunya) of independent existence because they arise dependently; emptiness is not a hidden substance but the absence of intrinsic nature.
Jainism holds that reality is complex and many-sided (anekanta): any statement captures only some aspects, so claims should be qualified by standpoint.
Kashmir Shaivism treats the world as the real, self-expression of consciousness (Shiva) through its own power (Shakti), not as illusion.

startHere.note: The Gita's compressed criterion: what is unreal has no being, and what is real never ceases to be.

goDeeper.note: Krishna's two natures: the lower eightfold prakriti and the higher conscious nature.
